hello.title: Hello, Nim
hello.summary: Write your first Nim program, print text and numbers with echo, and compile and run it.
hello.lesson.0: Nim is a programming language that is easy to read and creates fast programs. A Nim program is a text file that ends in `.nim`. The command `echo` prints a line of text.
hello.lesson.2: Text in double quotes, like `"Hello, Nim!"`, is a **string**. Nim runs the lines from top to bottom, and every `echo` prints its own line. You do not need a `main` function: the code at the top level of the file is the program.
hello.lesson.5: Nim is a **compiled** language: a compiler turns your code into a program that the computer can run. Save the code as `hello.nim` and run `nim c -r hello.nim` in a terminal. `c` compiles the file, and `-r` runs the program right after compiling it.
hello.lesson.6: `echo` can print several values: separate them with commas. Nim prints them directly one after the other and does not add spaces, so put the spaces into your strings. Numbers have no quotes, and Nim calculates `2 + 3` before it prints the result.
hello.lesson.8: A `#` starts a **comment**. Nim ignores everything from `#` to the end of the line. `echo ""` prints an empty line.
hello.lesson.10: Nim also understands `nim r hello.nim`, which compiles and runs in one step. In this course, every program is short, and you can run each one with either command.
hello-1.explain: Nim prints with `echo`. The other commands come from other languages and do not exist in Nim.
hello-2.explain: The string is printed as it is. `3 + 4` has no quotes, so Nim calculates it and prints `7`.
hello-3.explain: `echo` prints the values directly one after the other. It prints `ab`.
hello-4.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `Hello, world!`.
hello-4.explain: `echo` prints a value and ends the line.
hello-5.explain: `echo` prints the string and then the result of `5 + 7`. A comma separates the two values.
hello-6.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `Ready`, then `Set`, then `Go!`.
hello-6.explain: Nim runs the lines from top to bottom, so the first line prints first.
hello-7.explain: `*` multiplies, so Nim prints `42`. Everything after `#` is a comment.
hello-8.explain: `"1 + 1"` is a string, so Nim prints the text as it is and does not calculate it. The quotes are not printed.
hello-9.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
hello-10.prompt: This program does not compile. Which line has the bug?
hello-10.explain: The string on this line has no closing quote. Write `echo "Middle"`.
hello-11.prompt: This program should print three lines. Which line has the bug?
hello-12.statement: A Nim program needs a `main` function to run.
hello-12.explain: The code at the top level of a `.nim` file is the program. `echo "Hi"` alone is a complete program.
variables.title: Variables and types
variables.summary: Store values with var, let and const, and get to know int, float, string and bool.
variables.lesson.0: A **variable** stores a value under a name. `var` creates a variable that you can change later. `=` gives it a value. Nim sees the value and chooses the type for you: this is called **type inference**.
variables.lesson.2: `let` creates a variable that keeps its first value: you cannot change it later. Use `let` whenever a value stays the same. `const` creates a **constant**, a value that the compiler must know before the program runs, like a fixed limit.
variables.lesson.4: Giving a `let` variable or a constant a new value is an error. After `let name = "Ada"`, the line `name = "Bob"` does not compile.
variables.lesson.6: The basic types are `int` (whole numbers like `42`), `float` (numbers with a decimal point like `2.5`), `string` (text) and `bool` (`true` or `false`). You can write the type after a colon: `var age: int = 30`. A `var` without a value gets a default: `0`, `0.0`, `""` or `false`.
variables.lesson.8: A variable keeps its type. After `var x = 5`, the line `x = "five"` does not compile, because `x` is an `int`. `typeof(x)` gives the type of `x`. The type `float` is also called `float64`.
variables.lesson.10: `+`, `-` and `*` calculate as usual. `/` always gives a `float`, even for two `int` values. `div` divides whole numbers and drops the rest, and `mod` gives the rest (the remainder).
variables.lesson.12: Nim does not mix `int` and `float` variables in one calculation. Convert an `int` with `float(x)` first. `int(x)` turns a `float` into an `int` and drops the decimal part.
variables.card.1: `const limit = 10` is known before the program runs
variables-1.explain: `x` starts at 4. `x = x + 3` stores 4 + 3, so `x` is 7.
variables-2.prompt: Which keyword creates a variable that keeps its first value and cannot change?
variables-2.explain: A `let` variable cannot get a new value. A `var` variable can. `mut` and `val` are not Nim keywords.
variables-3.explain: 5 fits 3 times into 17, so `17 div 5` is 3. The rest is 17 - 15 = 2, so `17 mod 5` is 2.
variables-4.explain: `/` always gives a `float`, even for two `int` values. 9 / 2 is `4.5`.
variables-5.statement: `var count: int` without a value gives `count` the value `0`.
variables-5.explain: A `var` without a value gets the default of its type. For `int` the default is `0`.
variables-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints the remainder of 10 divided by 3.
variables-6.explain: `mod` gives the remainder: 10 = 3 * 3 + 1, so it prints `1`. `div` would give 3.
variables-7.prompt: The program should print `Ana`, then `Ben`, but it does not compile. Which line must you change?
variables-7.explain: A `let` variable cannot get a new value. Create it with `var name = "Ana"`.
variables-8.prompt: Build the line that creates a constant `limit` with the value `50`.
variables-8.explain: `const` creates a constant, and `=` gives it its value.
variables-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `15`.
variables-9.explain: 10 * 2 is 20, and 20 - 5 is 15. In the other order you get (10 - 5) * 2 = 10.
variables-10.prompt: Match the type or operator with its meaning.
variables-11.prompt: This program does not compile. Which line has the error?
variables-11.explain: Nim does not multiply an `int` by a `float`. Convert first: `float(apples) * price`.
variables-12.explain: `5` makes `price` an `int`, and an `int` variable cannot hold `2.5`. Write `var price = 5.0` instead.
strings.title: Strings
strings.summary: Join strings with &, convert values with $, and use len, indexes and the tools in strutils.
strings.lesson.0: The operator `&` joins two strings into one new string.
strings.lesson.2: `&` only joins strings. To add a number, first turn it into a string with `$`. The `$` operator converts almost any value into a string.
strings.lesson.4: `"Age: " & age` does not compile, because `age` is an `int`. Write `"Age: " & $age`.
strings.lesson.5: `len` gives the number of characters. `s[0]` is the first character: the first index is `0`. `s[^1]` is the last character. A single character has the type `char` and is written in single quotes, like `'N'`.
strings.lesson.8: Many string tools are in the module `std/strutils`. The line `import std/strutils` at the top of the file makes them available. You can call them as `toUpperAscii(city)` or, shorter, as `city.toUpperAscii`. `contains` checks if a string contains another string, and `replace` replaces text.
strings.lesson.10: `add` appends text to the end of a `var` string. `s &= "c"` does the same as `s = s & "c"`.
strings.lesson.12: `s[1..3]` takes the characters from index `1` to index `3`, both included: `"hello"[1..3]` is `"ell"`. Upper and lower case are different characters: `"Nim".contains("nim")` is `false`.
strings.card.1: `$42` turns a value into a string
strings-1.explain: `&` joins the two strings without a space.
strings-2.explain: `&` only joins strings, and `n` is an `int`. You need `"n = " & $n`.
strings-3.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `Total: 12`.
strings-3.explain: `$total` turns the `int` into the string `"12"`, and `&` can join it.
strings-5.explain: Indexes start at 0: `s[0]` is `N`, so `s[1]` is `i`.
strings-6.explain: Upper and lower case are different characters. The text contains `World`, not `world`.
strings-7.explain: `toUpperAscii` is in the module `std/strutils`. Without the import, Nim does not know it.
strings-8.prompt: Build the line that prints `Hi, Ana`. The variable `name` holds `"Ana"`.
strings-8.explain: `&` joins the string `"Hi, "` and the string in `name`.
strings-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `abcabc`.
strings-9.explain: First `s` becomes `abc`, then `s & s` doubles it. In the other order you get `ababc`.
strings-10.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
strings-11.prompt: This program does not compile. Which line has the bug?
strings-11.explain: `count` is an `int`, and `&` only joins strings. Write `$count`.
strings-12.explain: `s[1..3]` takes the characters with index 1, 2 and 3, both ends included: `e`, `l`, `l`.
conditions.title: Decisions
conditions.summary: Let your program decide with if, elif and else, combine conditions with and, or, not, and use case.
conditions.lesson.0: `if` runs code only when a condition is `true`. The condition ends with a colon `:`. The lines that belong to the `if` are **indented**: they start with 2 spaces. The first line without the indentation is no longer part of the `if`.
conditions.lesson.2: Comparisons give a `bool`: `==` (equal), `!=` (not equal), `<`, `>`, `<=` (less or equal) and `>=` (greater or equal).
conditions.lesson.4: `elif` checks another condition when the ones before were `false`. `else` runs when no condition was `true`. Nim checks from top to bottom and runs only the first matching branch.
conditions.lesson.6: `and` is `true` when both sides are `true`. `or` is `true` when at least one side is `true`. `not` turns `true` into `false` and `false` into `true`.
conditions.lesson.8: `=` gives a value, `==` compares. `if x = 5:` does not compile. Write `if x == 5:`.
conditions.lesson.10: `case` compares one value with several `of` branches. A branch can list several values, like `of 6, 7:`, or a range, like `of 1..5:` (1 to 5). `else` covers all other values. Nim checks that every possible value is covered, so for numbers and strings you almost always need `else`.
conditions.lesson.12: `case` also works with strings: `of "yes", "y":` runs when the string is `"yes"` or `"y"`.
conditions-1.explain: 8 is not greater than 10, but it is greater than 5, so the `elif` branch runs.
conditions-2.explain: `5 >= 5` is `true`, but `3 > 4` is `false`. `and` needs both sides to be `true`.
conditions-3.statement: A `case` on an `int` needs an `else` branch when the `of` branches do not cover every possible value.
conditions-3.explain: Nim checks that every value is covered. Without `else`, a `case` on an `int` does not compile.
conditions-4.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `Adult` for the age 18.
conditions-4.explain: `>=` means greater or equal, so 18 counts. With `>` nothing is printed, and `=` does not compile.
conditions-5.explain: 4 is in the range `3..6`, so the second branch runs.
conditions-6.prompt: This program does not compile. Which line has the bug?
conditions-6.explain: `=` gives a value. To compare, use `==`: `if x == 3:`.
conditions-7.prompt: Build the line that checks that `age` is at least 18 and less than 65.
conditions-7.explain: `and` combines the two comparisons. The line ends with a colon.
conditions-8.prompt: Put the lines in order: the program prints `hot` above 25, `mild` above 10 and `cold` otherwise.
conditions-8.explain: `if` comes first, then `elif`, then `else`. Each `echo` is indented below its condition.
conditions-9.prompt: Match the operator with its meaning.
conditions-10.prompt: Which keyword checks a second condition after an `if`?
conditions-10.explain: Nim uses `elif`. The other spellings come from other languages and do not compile in Nim.
conditions-11.prompt: This program does not compile. Which line has the bug?
conditions-11.explain: The condition of an `if` must end with a colon: `if score > 50:`.
conditions-12.explain: `a or b` is `true` because `a` is `true`. `not a` is `false`.
loops.title: Loops
loops.summary: Repeat code with for and while, count up and down with ranges, and control loops with break and continue.
loops.lesson.0: A `for` loop repeats code. `for i in 1..3:` runs the indented lines once for each number from 1 to 3. `1..3` is a **range**, and both ends are included. In each round, `i` holds the current number.
loops.lesson.2: `..<` leaves out the end: `0..<3` gives `0`, `1` and `2`.
loops.lesson.4: `countdown(3, 1)` counts backwards from 3 to 1. `countup(0, 10, 5)` counts up in steps of 5: `0`, `5`, `10`.
loops.lesson.6: Loops often add up values. `total += n` is short for `total = total + n`. The same short form exists for `-=` and `*=`.
loops.lesson.9: A `while` loop repeats as long as its condition is `true`. Make sure that something in the loop changes the condition, otherwise the loop never ends.
loops.lesson.11: `break` leaves the loop at once. `continue` skips the rest of the current round and starts the next one.
loops.lesson.13: A `for` loop can also visit every character of a string: `for c in "Nim":` gives `'N'`, `'i'` and `'m'`.
loops-3.explain: `countdown(3, 1)` gives 3, 2, 1, and each number is added to the end of `s`.
loops-4.statement: `for i in 1..5:` runs the loop body 5 times.
loops-4.explain: The range `1..5` includes both ends: 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5.
loops-5.prompt: Complete the loop so it prints 1, 2 and 3.
loops-6.prompt: This program does not compile. Which line has the bug?
loops-6.explain: The `for` line must end with a colon: `for i in 1..3:`.
loops-7.prompt: Build the line that repeats the loop as long as `n` is less than 100.
loops-7.explain: `while` repeats while the condition is `true`. The line ends with a colon.
loops-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints only the even numbers from 1 to 5.
loops-8.explain: For odd numbers, `continue` skips the `echo`. So the check must come before `echo i`.
loops-9.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
loops-10.explain: `n` becomes 3, 6, 9 and 12. Only at 12 is `n < 10` false, so the loop stops.
loops-11.explain: 5 * 5 = 25 is not greater than 30, but 6 * 6 = 36 is. So the loop stops at 6, and `last` is 5.
loops-12.prompt: This program should count down from 5 to 1, but it prints no numbers. Which line has the bug?
loops-12.explain: A range like `5..1` is empty, because it only counts up. Use `countdown(5, 1)`.
procs.title: Procedures
procs.summary: Write your own procedures with parameters and return types, use result, and call them with dot syntax.
procs.lesson.0: A **procedure** (`proc`) is a named block of code that you can run many times. You write `proc`, a name, parentheses, `=` and the indented body. To run, or **call**, the procedure, write its name with parentheses.
procs.lesson.2: **Parameters** are inputs. Each one has a name and a type, like `name: string`. Separate parameters with commas. When you call the procedure, you pass a value for each parameter.
procs.lesson.4: A procedure can give back a value. Write the return type after the parentheses, like `: int`. `return` gives back a value and ends the procedure. When the body is one expression, its value is returned.
procs.lesson.6: `a, b: int` gives both parameters the type `int`. Every procedure with a return type also has a hidden variable called `result`. It starts with the default value of the type, and its value at the end is returned. Most Nim code uses `result`.
procs.lesson.8: Nim does not let you ignore a returned value. The line `add(2, 3)` alone does not compile. Use the value, or write `discard add(2, 3)` to throw it away.
procs.lesson.10: `x.f(y)` is the same as `f(x, y)`: the value before the dot becomes the first parameter. Without other parameters, you can leave out the parentheses: `x.f`. This is why `word.len` and `city.toUpperAscii` work.
procs.lesson.12: Parameters are read-only inside the procedure. To change a variable of the caller, write `var` before the type of the parameter. You can only pass a `var` variable to it.
procs.card.0: `proc add(a, b: int): int = a + b`
procs-2.explain: `result` starts at 1 and is doubled three times: 2, 4, 8.
procs-3.prompt: Complete the header so the procedure returns an `int`.
procs-3.explain: The return type comes after the parentheses and a colon: `: int`.
procs-4.statement: In a procedure with a return type, you can use `result` without declaring it.
procs-4.explain: Nim creates `result` for you. Its value at the end is returned.
procs-5.prompt: The program should print `5`, but it does not compile. Which line has the bug?
procs-5.explain: The returned value is not used, and Nim does not allow that. Print it: `echo add(2, 3)`.
procs-6.explain: `"Bo".greet` is the same as `greet("Bo")`, which returns `"Hi Bo"`.
procs-7.prompt: Build the header of a procedure `isEven` with an `int` parameter `n` that returns a `bool`.
procs-7.explain: `proc`, the name with the parameters, a colon with the return type, and `=`.
procs-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints the larger number, `7`.
procs-8.explain: The `if` and the second `return` are the body of the procedure. `return a` belongs to the `if`.
procs-9.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
procs-9.pairs.3: a parameter the procedure can change
procs-10.explain: `x` is a `var` parameter, so each call changes `a`: 1, then 3, then 5.
procs-11.prompt: This program does not compile. Which line must you change?
procs-11.explain: Parameters are read-only. Write `n: var int` so the procedure can change the variable.
procs-12.explain: The loop visits every character, and `banana` contains the character `a` three times.
collections.title: Arrays and sequences
collections.summary: Keep many values in arrays and sequences: read, change, add and loop over elements.
collections.lesson.0: An **array** holds a fixed number of values of the same type. You write it in square brackets: `[10, 20, 30]`. Its type is `array[3, int]`: the length is part of the type. `nums[0]` is the first element, and `len` gives the number of elements.
collections.lesson.2: A **sequence** (`seq`) can grow. `@[...]` creates one, and `add` puts a value at the end. The type of a sequence of strings is `seq[string]`. A `var` sequence without a value starts empty.
collections.lesson.4: Like with strings, `s[^1]` is the last element. `in` checks if a value is in an array or a sequence.
collections.lesson.6: An index that does not exist stops the program with an error (`IndexDefect`). With four elements, `primes[4]` fails, because the last index is `3`.
collections.lesson.8: `for x in s:` visits every element. `for i, x in s:` also gives you the index: `i` is the index and `x` the element.
collections.lesson.10: With a loop, you can add up all elements. Start with `0.0` when the elements are `float` values.
collections.lesson.12: `for i in 0..<s.len:` also visits every index. The last index is always `s.len - 1`.
collections.card.4: `x in s` checks if x is in s
collections-1.explain: After `add` the sequence has 3 elements, and the last one is 15.
collections-2.explain: Indexes start at 0, so index 1 is the second element, `y`.
collections-3.statement: In `for i, x in s:`, `i` is the element and `x` is the index.
collections-3.explain: The index comes first: `i` is the index and `x` is the element.
collections-4.prompt: Complete the code so `nums` is a sequence that can grow.
collections-4.explain: `@[1, 2]` creates a sequence. Without `@` it would be an array, and arrays have no `add`.
collections-6.prompt: This program stops with an `IndexDefect` error. Which line has the bug?
collections-6.explain: `0..nums.len` includes 3, but the last index is 2. Use `0..<nums.len`.
collections-7.prompt: Build the line that creates an empty sequence of strings called `names`.
collections-7.explain: `var names: seq[string]` creates a sequence variable without elements.
collections-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program collects the even numbers from 1 to 6 and prints `@[2, 4, 6]`.
collections-8.explain: Create the empty sequence first, add each even number in the loop, and print after the loop.
collections-9.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
collections-10.explain: `i` is the index. The element 6 has index 1.
collections-11.explain: `words[0] = "c"` replaces `a`, and `add` puts `d` at the end.
collections-12.prompt: The program should print `4`, but it does not compile. Which line must you change?
collections-12.explain: `a` is an array, and an array cannot grow. Make it a sequence: `var a = @[1, 2, 3]`.
objects.title: Objects
objects.summary: Define your own object types with fields, create and change objects, and write procedures for them.
objects.lesson.0: An **object** type groups values that belong together. Each value is a **field** with a name and a type. You define object types in a `type` section. Type names start with a capital letter. `Book(title: "Dune", pages: 412)` creates a `Book`, and `b.title` reads a field.
objects.lesson.2: `echo` prints an object with all its fields in parentheses. In a `var` object, you can change a field with `=`. `x, y: int` creates two fields of the type `int`.
objects.lesson.4: Fields that you leave out get the default value of their type, like `0` for an `int`.
objects.lesson.6: The fields of a `let` object cannot change. After `let p = Point(x: 1, y: 2)`, the line `p.x = 3` does not compile.
objects.lesson.8: A procedure can take an object as a parameter. With dot syntax, `r.area` is the same as `area(r)`, so the procedure looks like a part of the object.
objects.lesson.10: To change an object inside a procedure, use a `var` parameter, as you did with numbers.
objects.lesson.12: Objects work well together with sequences. A `seq[Item]` holds many `Item` objects, and a loop can visit each one.
objects.card.0: `type Point = object` with fields like `x: int`
objects.card.2: `p.x` reads a field, `p.x = 5` changes it (`var` only)
objects.card.3: `proc area(r: Rect): int` is called as `r.area`
objects.card.4: `proc grow(r: var Rect)` can change the object
objects-1.explain: `d.name` is `Rex` and `d.age` is 3. `echo` prints the three values one after the other.
objects-2.explain: `y` starts at 0 because it was left out. Then `p.y = p.x * 3` sets it to 6.
objects-3.statement: Fields that you leave out when you create an object get their default value, like `0` for an `int`.
objects-3.explain: Every field you do not set starts with the default value of its type.
objects-4.prompt: Complete the code so it creates a `Circle`.
objects-4.explain: You create an object with the type name and the fields in parentheses: `Circle(radius: 2.0)`. The capital letter matters.
objects-5.prompt: The program should print `10`, but it does not compile. Which line has the bug?
objects-5.explain: The fields of a `let` object cannot change. Create it with `var p = Point(x: 1, y: 2)`.
objects-7.prompt: Build the line that creates a `Point` `p` with `x` 3 and `y` 4.
objects-7.explain: Write the type name, then the fields with `name: value` in parentheses, separated by commas.
objects-8.prompt: Put the lines in order: first the type, then the procedure, then the code that uses it. The program prints `6`.
objects-8.explain: The type comes first. `bump` adds 1 to `value`, so you must call it before `echo` to print 6.
objects-9.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
objects-9.pairs.4: a parameter the procedure can change
objects-10.explain: The parameter `p` is read-only. To change it, the procedure needs `p: var Person`.
objects-11.prompt: This program does not compile. Which line has the bug?
objects-11.explain: `Item` has no field `cost`. The field is called `price`: `pen.price`.
objects-12.explain: The loop keeps the person with the highest age. Ben is 41, the oldest.
